claim: Huntington's disease (HD) is mainly caused by cytotoxicity of the mutant huntingtin protein (Htt) with an expanded polyQ stretch.
source: Huntington's disease (HD) represents an important model for neurodegenerative disorders and proteinopathies. It is mainly caused by cytotoxicity of the mutant huntingtin protein (Htt) with an expanded polyQ stretch.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations in the introduction section (Rubinsztein and Carmichael, 2003).

claim: While Htt is ubiquitously expressed, HD is characterized by selective neurodegeneration of the striatum.
source: While Htt is ubiquitously expressed, HD is characterized by selective neurodegeneration of the striatum.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations in the introduction (Cowan and Raymond, 2006).

claim: Gpr52 is a striatal-enriched orphan G protein-coupled receptor that acts as a stabilizer of Htt in vitro and in vivo.
source: Here we report a striatal-enriched orphan G protein-coupled receptor(GPCR) Gpr52 as a stabilizer of Htt in vitro and in vivo.
evidence: This is the main finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Gpr52 modulates Htt via cAMP-dependent but PKA independent mechanisms.
source: Gpr52 modulates Htt via cAMP-dependent but PKA independent mechanisms.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 3D showing that PKA inhibitors do not block Gpr52's effect while cAMP analogs do.

claim: Gpr52 is located within an intron of Rabgap1l.
source: Gpr52 is located within an intron of Rabgap1l, which exhibits epistatic effects on Gpr52-mediated modulation of Htt levels by inhibiting its substrate Rab39B, which co-localizes with Htt and translocates Htt to the endoplasmic reticulum.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by genomic data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Rabgap1l exhibits epistatic effects on Gpr52-mediated modulation of Htt levels.
source: Gpr52 is located within an intron of Rabgap1l, which exhibits epistatic effects on Gpr52-mediated modulation of Htt levels by inhibiting its substrate Rab39B, which co-localizes with Htt and translocates Htt to the endoplasmic reticulum.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 4A showing that Rabgap1l knockdown blunts Gpr52's effect on Htt levels.

claim: Rab39B co-localizes with Htt and translocates Htt to the endoplasmic reticulum.
source: Gpr52 is located within an intron of Rabgap1l, which exhibits epistatic effects on Gpr52-mediated modulation of Htt levels by inhibiting its substrate Rab39B, which co-localizes with Htt and translocates Htt to the endoplasmic reticulum.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 4C showing increased co-localization of Htt and Rab39B upon cAMP analog treatment.

claim: Reducing Gpr52 suppresses HD phenotypes in patient iPS-derived neurons.
source: Finally, reducing Gpr52 suppresses HD phenotypes in both patient iPS-derived neurons and in vivo Drosophila HD models.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 5B-C showing reduced caspase 3 activity and neuronal loss upon Gpr52 knockdown.

claim: Reducing Gpr52 suppresses HD phenotypes in in vivo Drosophila HD models.
source: Finally, reducing Gpr52 suppresses HD phenotypes in both patient iPS-derived neurons and in vivo Drosophila HD models.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 5D showing improved motor performance in Drosophila HD models with Gpr52 knockdown.

claim: Transfection of Gpr52 siRNAs in mouse striatal cells (STHdhQ7/Q111) lowers Htt levels.
source: Transfection of Gpr52 siRNAs (Gpr52_si1∼3) in the mouse striatal cells (STHdhQ7/Q111) lowers Htt levels, as detected by Htt antibodies MW1, 2166, ab1 and 2B7.
evidence: This is stated in the Figure 1A legend and shown in the western blots and quantification in Figure 1A.

claim: Infection of lentiviruses expressing Gpr52 shRNAs lowers Htt in primary striatal but not cortical neurons cultured from HdhQ140/Q140 knock-in mice.
source: Infection of lentiviruses expressing Gpr52 shRNAs (Gpr52_sh1∼2) lowers Htt in primary striatal but not cortical neurons cultured from HdhQ140/Q140 knock-in mice.
evidence: This is stated in the Figure 1B legend and shown in the western blots and quantification in Figure 1B.

claim: Heterozygous knockout of Gpr52 lowers Htt in vivo in the striata but not cortices of HdhQ140/Q7 knock-in mice.
source: Heterozygous knockout of Gpr52 lowers Htt in vivo in the striata but not cortices of HdhQ140/Q7 knock-in mice in vivo.
evidence: This is stated in the Figure 1C legend and shown in the western blots and quantification in Figure 1C.

claim: Transfection of human Gpr52 siRNAs in HD patient iPS-derived neurons lowers Htt levels.
source: Transfection of human Gpr52 siRNAs (hGpr52_si1∼2) in the HD patient iPS-derived neurons lowers Htt levels detected by both western-blots and HTRF.
evidence: This is stated in the Figure 1D legend and shown in the western blots and HTRF quantification in Figure 1D.

claim: HD patient iPS-derived striatal-like neurons express molecular markers for striatal medium spiny neurons: Tuj1, GABA and DARPP32.
source: Differentiated neurons from HD patient's iPS cells express molecular markers for striatal medium spiny neurons: Tuj1, GABA and DARPP32.
evidence: This is stated in the Figure 1D legend and shown in the immunostaining images in Figure 1D.

claim: Gpr52 knock-down does not reduce Ataxin3 levels.
source: Representative western-blots of STHdhQ7/Q111 cell lysates showing no reduction of Ataxin3 levels by Gpr52 knock-down.
evidence: This is stated in the Figure 2A legend and shown in the western blots and quantification in Figure 2A.

claim: The Htt reduction by Gpr52 knock-down is not due to protein cleavage modulations.
source: Full membrane images of Htt blots showing no increase/appearance of lower molecular weight bands in the STHdh cell lysates, suggesting that the Htt reduction by Gpr52 knock-down is not due to protein cleavage modulations.
evidence: This is stated in the Figure 2B legend and shown in the full membrane images in Figure 2B.

claim: Gpr52 knock-down reduces Htt levels in both the P2 and S2 fractions, but not the P1 fraction.
source: Gpr52 knock-down reduced Htt levels in both the P2 and S2 fractions, but not the P1 fraction.
evidence: This is stated in the Figure 2C legend and shown in the western blots in Figure 2C.

claim: Gpr52 knock-down does not reduce Htt mRNA levels.
source: In the Gpr52 siRNAs (triangles) transfected STHdhQ7/Q111 cells, Htt mRNA levels (Y-axis) and Gpr52 mRNA (X-axis) levels were measured by qPCR. Both the Gpr52 siRNAs and the Htt siRNAs show substantial knock-down of their targets, whereas the Gpr52 knock-down by Gpr52 siRNAs do not reduce Htt mRNA levels.
evidence: This is stated in the Figure 2D legend and shown in the qPCR data in Figure 2D.

claim: The Htt lowering by Gpr52 knock-down is completely blocked by treatment with proteasome inhibitors.
source: In addition, the Htt mRNA level is not affected by Gpr52 (Figure 2D), and the Gpr52's effect is completely blocked by treatment with proteasome inhibitors (Figure 2E), suggesting that the modulation is mainly mediated by proteasomal degradation.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in the western blots and quantification in Figure 2E.

claim: The modulation of Htt by Gpr52 is mainly mediated by proteasomal degradation.
source: In addition, the Htt mRNA level is not affected by Gpr52 (Figure 2D), and the Gpr52's effect is completely blocked by treatment with proteasome inhibitors (Figure 2E), suggesting that the modulation is mainly mediated by proteasomal degradation.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing no change in Htt mRNA and complete blockade by proteasome inhibitors.

claim: Over-expression of Gpr52 cDNA leads to a dose-dependent increase of Htt.
source: Consistent with this, over-expression of Gpr52 cDNA (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) or treatment with an agonist reserpine (Komatsu et al., 2014) (Figure 3A) leads to a dose-dependent increase of Htt (Figure 3B–C), confirming Gpr52 as an Htt stabilizer.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in the HTRF data in Figure 3C and western blots in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Treatment with the Gpr52 agonist reserpine leads to a dose-dependent increase of Htt.
source: Consistent with this, over-expression of Gpr52 cDNA (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) or treatment with an agonist reserpine (Komatsu et al., 2014) (Figure 3A) leads to a dose-dependent increase of Htt (Figure 3B–C), confirming Gpr52 as an Htt stabilizer.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in the HTRF data in Figure 3B.

claim: Gpr52 is a Gαs-coupled receptor that increases intracellular cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) levels when activated.
source: As a Gαs-coupled receptor, Gpr52 increases intracellular cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) levels when activated (Komatsu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citation.

claim: The intracellular cAMP level is reduced by knocking-down Gpr52.
source: Consistent with this, the intracellular cAMP level is reduced by knocking-down Gpr52 (by 15.6 ± 2.5 nM, 35.8 ± 2.5 nM and 21.1 ± 3.1 nM, respectively; Figure 3A), suggesting some levels of constitutive activity.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in the cAMP measurement data in Figure 3A.

claim: Treatment of forskolin completely inhibits the Htt reduction caused by the Gpr52 knock-down.
source: Treatment of forskolin completely inhibits the Htt reduction caused by the Gpr52 knock-down (Figure 3D, left panel, lane 5 and 6 compared to lane 1 and 2; Bar plot), suggesting that the reduction of cAMP is required for the Gpr52 mediated Htt modulation.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in the western blots and HTRF data in Figure 3D.

claim: The reduction of cAMP is required for the Gpr52 mediated Htt modulation.
source: Treatment of forskolin completely inhibits the Htt reduction caused by the Gpr52 knock-down (Figure 3D, left panel, lane 5 and 6 compared to lane 1 and 2; Bar plot), suggesting that the reduction of cAMP is required for the Gpr52 mediated Htt modulation.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing that forskolin, which increases cAMP, blocks Gpr52's effect.

claim: Rp-cAMP is a non-hydrolysable cAMP analog that does not activate PKA.
source: To test possible PKA-dependence, we treated the cells with Rp-cAMP, a non-hydrolysable cAMP analog that does not activate PKA (Rothermel and Parker Botelho, 1988) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citation and PKA activity data in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Rp-cAMP completely inhibits the Gpr52's effect on Htt levels.
source: Rp-cAMP completely inhibits the Gpr52's effect on Htt levels (Figure 3D, middle panel, lane 5 and 6 compared to lane 1 and 2; bar plot), indicating that the Htt reduction by knocking-down Gpr52 is mediated via a PKA-independent sensor of cAMP levels.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in the western blots and HTRF data in Figure 3D.

claim: The Htt reduction by knocking-down Gpr52 is mediated via a PKA-independent sensor of cAMP levels.
source: Rp-cAMP completely inhibits the Gpr52's effect on Htt levels (Figure 3D, middle panel, lane 5 and 6 compared to lane 1 and 2; bar plot), indicating that the Htt reduction by knocking-down Gpr52 is mediated via a PKA-independent sensor of cAMP levels.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing that Rp-cAMP, which does not activate PKA, blocks Gpr52's effect.

claim: 8-pCPT-2′-O-Me-cAMP is a cAMP analog that does not activate PKA.
source: Similarly, another cAMP analog 8-pCPT-2′-O-Me-cAMP that does not activate PKA (Enserink et al., 2002) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2) completely abolishes the Htt reduction (Figure 3D; Bar plot) as well.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citation and PKA activity data in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: 8-pCPT-2′-O-Me-cAMP completely abolishes the Htt reduction by Gpr52 knockdown.
source: Similarly, another cAMP analog 8-pCPT-2′-O-Me-cAMP that does not activate PKA (Enserink et al., 2002) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2) completely abolishes the Htt reduction (Figure 3D; Bar plot) as well.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in the HTRF data in Figure 3D.

claim: The PKA inhibitor H89 fails to inhibit the Htt reduction by Gpr52 knock-down.
source: In contrast, the PKA inhibitor H89 (Takuma and Ichida, 1994) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2) and a PKA-specific agonist 6-Bnz-cAMP (Christensen et al., 2003) fail to inhibit the Htt reduction by Gpr52 knock-down (Figure 3D), confirming the PKA-independence.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in the HTRF data in Figure 3D.

claim: The PKA-specific agonist 6-Bnz-cAMP fails to inhibit the Htt reduction by Gpr52 knock-down.
source: In contrast, the PKA inhibitor H89 (Takuma and Ichida, 1994) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2) and a PKA-specific agonist 6-Bnz-cAMP (Christensen et al., 2003) fail to inhibit the Htt reduction by Gpr52 knock-down (Figure 3D), confirming the PKA-independence.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in the HTRF data in Figure 3D.

claim: A sustained increase of the cAMP level is needed to abolish the Gpr52's effect on Htt.
source: Finally, the hydrolysable cAMP analog 8-Br-cAMP has little effect on the Gpr52 mediated Htt reduction (Figure 3D, middle panel, lane 3 and 4 compared to lane 1 and 2; bar plot), whereas the non-hydrolysable cAMP analogs 8-pCPT-2′-O-Me-cAMP and Rp-cAMP block the Gpr52's effect entirely (Figure 3D), indicating that a sustained increase of the cAMP level is needed to abolish the Gpr52's effect.
evidence: This is inferred from the data comparing hydrolysable and non-hydrolysable cAMP analogs in Figure 3D.

claim: Treatment with PKA-insensitive analogs Rp-cAMP or 8-pCPT-2′-O-Me cAMP leads to Htt enrichment at the perinuclear regions and co-localization with the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) marker.
source: Given that the major function of small GTPases is trafficking, we tested potential Htt translocation events upon treatments of PKA-insensitive analogs Rp-cAMP or 8-pCPT-2′-O-Me cAMP, and found that they lead to Htt enrichment at the perinuclear regions and co-localization with the endoplasmic reticulumn (ER) marker (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in the immunofluorescence images and quantification in Figure 3E.

claim: Translocation of Htt to the ER may prevent its proteasomal degradation due to lack of proteasomes in the ER.
source: Translocation of Htt to the ER may prevent its proteasomal degradation due to lack of proteasomes in the ER (Plemper et al., 1997).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citation.

claim: In the genomes of vertebrates including human, monkey, mouse, rat, dog, chicken and zebrafish, Gpr52 is a single exon gene that is located in the intron of another gene Rabgap1l.
source: In the genomes of vertebrates including human, monkey, mouse, rat, dog, chicken and zebrafish, Gpr52 is a single exon gene that is located in the intron of another gene Rabgap1l, which encodes a GTPase-activating protein (GAP) in the same orientation.
evidence: This is stated in the text and can be verified from genomic databases.

claim: Gpr52 is located within the intron of the GAP domain-containing splice variants (GAP transcripts) of Rabgap1l only, but not the non-GAP transcripts.
source: Gpr52 is located within the intron of the GAP domain-containing splice variants (GAP transcripts) only, but not the non-GAP transcripts (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), suggesting possible functional links.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in the genomic loci diagram in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Knocking-down Rabgap1l increases Htt levels.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, knocking-down Rabgap1l increases Htt levels (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B) and blunts the Gpr52's effect (Figure 4A, Htt lowering drops from 60.3 ± 7.1% to 6.3 ± 7.7%).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in the western blots and HTRF data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Knocking-down Rabgap1l blunts the Gpr52's effect on Htt levels.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, knocking-down Rabgap1l increases Htt levels (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B) and blunts the Gpr52's effect (Figure 4A, Htt lowering drops from 60.3 ± 7.1% to 6.3 ± 7.7%).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in the western blots and HTRF data in Figure 4A.

claim: Both Gpr52 and Rabgap1l mRNA levels are lowered when HTT is knocked-down.
source: Interestingly, both Gpr52 and Rabgap1l mRNA levels are lowered when HTT is knocked-down (Figure 4B, dark axis). As a control, Gapdh mRNA levels do not change (Figure 4B, blue axis).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in the qPCR data in Figure 4B.

claim: Gpr52 and Rabgap1l could be co-regulated together, possibly facilitated by their shared genomic locus, via possible feedback regulation by Htt.
source: This suggests that Gpr52 and Rabgap1l could be co-regulated together, possibly facilitated by their shared genomic locus, via possible feedback regulation by Htt.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing coordinated changes in Gpr52 and Rabgap1l mRNA levels upon HTT knockdown.

claim: There are three reported substrates for Rabgap1l: Rab22A, Rab39B and Rab34.
source: There are three reported substrates for Rabgap1l: Rab22A, Rab39B and Rab34 (Itoh et al., 2006), among which Rab22A and Rab39B are expressed in the brain (http://www.biogps.org/; http://www.brain-map.org/).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citation.

claim: Rab22A and Rab39B are expressed in the brain.
source: There are three reported substrates for Rabgap1l: Rab22A, Rab39B and Rab34 (Itoh et al., 2006), among which Rab22A and Rab39B are expressed in the brain (http://www.biogps.org/; http://www.brain-map.org/).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by references to gene expression databases.

claim: Rab39B but not Rab22A shows significantly increased co-localization with Htt when the cells are treated with cAMP analogs Rp-cAMP or 8-pCPT-2′-O-Me cAMP.
source: Interestingly, Rab39B but not Rab22A shows significantly increased co-localization with Htt when the cells are treated with cAMP analogs Rp-cAMP or 8-pCPT-2′-O-Me cAMP (Figure 4C; Figure 4—figure supplement 2), suggesting that Rab39B may participate in the translocation of Htt to the ER.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in the immunofluorescence images and quantification in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Expressing the constitutively active form of Rab39B blunts the Gpr52's effect on Htt levels.
source: Consistent with this, expressing the constitutively active form of Rab39B blunts the Gpr52's effect (averaged Htt lowering reduces from 54.1 ± 6.3% to 17.2 ± 10.6%), confirming Rab39B's involvement in the pathway (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in the western blots and quantification in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: Knocking-down Gpr52 remarkably reduces serum starvation-induced caspase 3 and/or 7 activity in STHdhQ111/Q111 cells.
source: Knocking-down Gpr52 remarkably reduces serum starvation-induced caspase 3 and/or 7 activity in STHdhQ111/Q111 cells (by 67.8 ± 1.1%; Figure 5A), indicating a suppression of the mHTT-induced toxicity.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in the caspase activity data in Figure 5A.

claim: Treatment of forskolin substantially blunts the suppression of caspase activity by Gpr52 knockdown.
source: Treatment of forskolin substantially blunts this effect (to 17.3 ± 4.8%; Figure 5A), confirming that the Gpr52's effect is mainly mediated via the cAMP-dependent Htt reduction.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in the caspase activity data in Figure 5A.

claim: In HD patient iPS-derived striatal neurons, knocking-down Gpr52 suppresses the mHtt-dependent neuronal loss and caspase 3 activation induced by withdrawn of BDNF.
source: Consistently, in the HD patient iPS-derived striatal neurons, knocking-down Gpr52 suppresses the mHtt-dependent neuronal loss and caspase 3 activation induced by withdrawn of the brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) (HD iPS Consortium, 2012; Lu and Palacino, 2013) (Figure 5B–C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in the immunofluorescence images and quantification in Figure 5B-C.

claim: Knocking-down Rabgap1l exacerbates the neuronal loss in HD patient iPS-derived neurons.
source: In addition, knocking-down Rabgap1l exacerbate the neuronal loss and attenuates Gpr52's rescue (Figure 5C), confirming the involvement of Rabgap1l.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in the quantification in Figure 5C.

claim: Knocking-down Rabgap1l attenuates Gpr52's rescue of neuronal loss in HD patient iPS-derived neurons.
source: In addition, knocking-down Rabgap1l exacerbate the neuronal loss and attenuates Gpr52's rescue (Figure 5C), confirming the involvement of Rabgap1l.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in the quantification in Figure 5C.

claim: Decreased levels of Drosophila Gpr52 by shRNA knockdown causes a robust suppression of the motor deficits induced by expression of NT-Htt128Q in the Drosophila central nervous system.
source: Decreased levels of Drosophila Gpr52 either by shRNA knockdown or by loss-of-function mutation (LOF) causes a robust suppression of the motor deficits induced by expression of this mHtt fragment in the Drosophila central nervous system (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in the motor performance data in Figure 5D.

claim: Decreased levels of Drosophila Gpr52 by loss-of-function mutation causes a robust suppression of the motor deficits induced by expression of NT-Htt128Q in the Drosophila central nervous system.
source: Decreased levels of Drosophila Gpr52 either by shRNA knockdown or by loss-of-function mutation (LOF) causes a robust suppression of the motor deficits induced by expression of this mHtt fragment in the Drosophila central nervous system (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in the motor performance data in Figure 5D.

claim: Knock-down of the Drosophila homolog of Rabgap1l exacerbates the HD motor deficits in the in vivo fly model.
source: Meanwhile, consistent with cellular models where Rabgap1l functions in opposition to the effect of Gpr52, knock-down of the Drosophila homolog of Rabgap1l exacerbates the HD motor deficits in the in vivo fly model (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in the motor performance data in Figure 5D.

claim: Expression of Gpr52 shRNA substantially improves the motor defects in Drosophila expressing full length human Htt protein with 200Q (FL-Htt200Q).
source: The rescue effect by knocking-down Gpr52 is further validated in a Drosophila model of HD expressing the full length human Htt protein with 200Q (FL-Htt200Q). Expression of Gpr52 shRNA substantially improves the motor defects in those flies as well (Video 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Video 1 and Figure 5D.

claim: Gpr52 has been recently characterized as a Gαs-coupled receptor highly enriched in the striatum, especially D2 neurons.
source: Second, Gpr52 has been recently characterized as a Gαs-coupled receptor highly enriched in the striatum, especially D2 neurons (Sawzdargo et al., 1999; Komatsu et al., 2014), which are amongst the earliest affected in HD (Raymond et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citations.

claim: D2 neurons are amongst the earliest affected in HD.
source: Second, Gpr52 has been recently characterized as a Gαs-coupled receptor highly enriched in the striatum, especially D2 neurons (Sawzdargo et al., 1999; Komatsu et al., 2014), which are amongst the earliest affected in HD (Raymond et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citation.

claim: The coincidence between Gpr52 expression and selective neurodegeneration suggests that Gpr52 may contribute to the selective early loss of striatal neurons in HD.
source: The coincidence between Gpr52 expression and selective neurodegeneration suggests that Gpr52 may contribute to the selective early loss of striatal neurons in HD.
evidence: This is stated in the text as a speculation based on the expression pattern and disease pathology.

claim: STHdhQ7/Q111 cells are a well-established and easily-transfectable striatal-derived cellular HD model expressing endogenous full length mHtt.
source: To identify modulators of Htt levels in the striatal cells, we screened through a number of candidates in STHdhQ7/Q111 cells, a well-established and easily-transfectable striatal-derived cellular HD model expressing endogenous full length mHtt (Trettel et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citation.

claim: The screening identified six potential modulators of mHtt levels: Gpr52 and Eaf1 siRNAs lower mHtt, whereas Gclc, Grid2, Ndrg3 and Hdhd3 siRNAs increase its level.
source: This effort revealed six potential modulators of mHtt levels: Gpr52 and Eaf1 siRNAs lower mHtt, whereas Gclc, Grid2, Ndrg3 and Hdhd3 siRNAs increase its level (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in the western blots and quantification in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: GPCRs locate on the plasma membrane and their functions are modulated by extracellular molecules, placing them among the most druggable targets.
source: First, GPCRs locate on the plasma membrane and their functions are modulated by extracellular molecules, placing them among the most druggable targets: highly accessible to drugs and the functions are modulated by small molecules.
evidence: This is stated in the text as general knowledge about GPCRs.

claim: The mutant Htt protein (mHtt) is expressed throughout the brain and peripheral tissues, but elicits selective neurodegeneration of the corpus striatum and lesser damage to the cerebral cortex in HD patients.
source: The major cause of HD is the cytotoxicity of the mutant Htt protein (mHtt) (Rubinsztein and Carmichael, 2003), which is expressed throughout the brain and peripheral tissues, but elicits selective neurodegeneration of the corpus striatum and lesser damage to the cerebral cortex in HD patients (Cowan and Raymond, 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citations.

claim: The selective neurodegeneration in HD is likely contributed, at least partially, by striatal-enriched modulators of mHtt toxicity and stability.
source: This selectivity is likely contributed, at least partially, by striatal-enriched modulators of mHtt toxicity and stability (Subramaniam et al., 2009; Tsvetkov et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citations.

claim: The neuronal longevity correlates with mHtt turnover, which is slower in striatal than in cortical neurons.
source: Consistent with this idea, the neuronal longevity correlates with mHtt turnover, which is slower in striatal than in cortical neurons (Tsvetkov et al., 2013), suggesting expression of striatal-enriched mHtt stabilizers.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citation.

claim: Lowering mHtt level should suppress its downstream toxicity and treat HD.
source: More importantly, it provides potential therapeutic entry points for HD: while the mechanism of mHtt toxicity is unclear, lowering its level should suppress its downstream toxicity and treat the disease (Yu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citation.

claim: Reducing the wild-type Htt protein (wtHtt) seems to be well-tolerated.
source: Meanwhile, reducing the wild-type Htt protein (wtHtt) at the same time seems to be well-tolerated (Boudreau et al., 2009; Grondin et al., 2012; Lu and Palacino, 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citations.

claim: Modulators of Htt levels are attractive targets for potential HD treatment.
source: Thus, modulators of Htt levels are attractive targets for potential HD treatment.
evidence: This is stated in the text as a conclusion based on the therapeutic rationale.

claim: STHdhQ111/Q111 cells exhibit mHtt-dependent caspase 3 and/or 7 activation by stress, such as serum removal.
source: STHdhQ111/Q111 cells exhibit mHtt-dependent caspase 3 and/or 7 activation by stress, such as serum removal (Miller et al., 2012; Lu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citations.

claim: The presence of Gpr52 leads to sustained elevation of intracellular cAMP levels, which activates potential GEF(s) and subsequently its substrate Rab39B.
source: Taken together (Figure 4D), the presence of Gpr52 leads to sustained elevation of intracellular cAMP levels, which activates potential GEF(s) and subsequently its substrate Rab39B.
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in the model in Figure 4D.

claim: Rab39B co-localizes with Htt and changes the localization of Htt, protecting it from degradation.
source: Rab39B co-localizes with Htt and changes the localization of Htt, protecting it from degradation.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by the co-localization data in Figure 4C.

claim: Rab39B is inactivated by its GAP Rabgap1l, which shows epistatic effects on Gpr52 mediated Htt modulation.
source: Rab39B is inactivated by its GAP Rabgap1l, which shows epistatic effects on Gpr52 mediated Htt modulation.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by the epistasis data in Figure 4A.

claim: Gpr52 and Rabgap1l locate in the same genomic loci, which may facilitate their balanced regulation of Htt levels in the striatal cells.
source: Gpr52 and Rabgap1l locate in the same genomic loci, which may facilitate their balanced regulation of Htt levels in the striatal cells.
evidence: This is stated in the text as a speculation based on the genomic organization.

claim: Gpr52 may contribute to the selective neurodegeneration in HD, although other mechanisms may contribute as well.
source: We have revealed Gpr52 as a striatal-enriched modulator of Htt levels. This provides a possible mechanism of selective neurodegeneration in the striatum, although other mechanisms may contribute as well; including striatal-enriched post-translational modifiers of Htt such as Rhes (Subramaniam et al., 2009), or non–cell-autonomous mechanisms (Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the text as a conclusion with acknowledgment of other possible mechanisms.

claim: Targeting Gpr52 is effective in lowering Htt and remarkably rescues HD phenotypes in vitro and in vivo.
source: Targeting Gpr52 is effective in lowering Htt and remarkably rescues HD phenotypes in vitro and in vivo (Figure 5), confirming its therapeutic potential.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by the rescue data in Figure 5.

claim: The sustained lowering of cAMP is required for GPCR-mediated lowering of endogenous soluble full-length Htt through PKA-independent mechanisms.
source: While the possible link between cAMP and Htt has been suggested previously (Williams et al., 2008; Lin et al., 2013), those studies focus on exogenously expressed or transgenic Htt aggregates or fragments, and show inconsistent results. Our data confirm that the sustained lowering of cAMP is required for GPCR-mediated lowering of endogenous soluble full-length Htt through PKA-independent mechanisms.
